title: FEC operates without a quorum for nearly 80% of Trump's second term
description_short: FEC operates without a quorum for nearly 80% of Trump's second term
description_medium: Trump sent longtime Democratic FEC commissioner Ellen Weintraub a January 31, 2025 letter purporting to remove her; Weintraub disputed the legality of the action. After additional commissioner departures, the FEC fell below its four-member voting threshold on May 1, 2025. NOTUS reported in March 2026 that the agency had 195 pending enforcement matters and later calculated that it had lacked a quorum for nearly 80% of Trump's second term. The prolonged lack of quorum prevented substantive enforcement votes.
description_long: Trump sent Democratic FEC commissioner Ellen Weintraub a January 31, 2025 letter purporting to remove her from office. Weintraub disputed the action's legality. Additional commissioner departures later left the agency below its four-member voting threshold on May 1, following Allen Dickerson's April 30 departure. The loss of quorum prevented substantive enforcement votes, creating an institutional consequence separate from the dispute over Weintraub's removal. NOTUS reported in March 2026 that 195 enforcement matters were pending and later calculated that the agency had lacked a quorum for nearly 80% of Trump's second term. These figures describe the scale and duration of the enforcement backlog; they do not establish the merits of every pending case. The supported explanation connects personnel changes to the agency's ability to act while keeping Weintraub's legal objection attributed to her. It does not imply that the backlog resulted solely from one removal or that all pending matters involved the president.

title: Trump Pardons Former Sheriff Joe Arpaio (2017)
description_short: Trump Pardons Former Sheriff Joe Arpaio (2017)
description_medium: On August 25, 2017, during his first term, President Donald Trump granted a full and unconditional pardon to Joe Arpaio, the former Maricopa County, Arizona sheriff convicted of criminal contempt for defying a federal court order in the Melendres v. Arpaio racial-profiling case. The pardon was issued via a White House press release and a signed warrant dated August 25, 2017. The card's date of January 20, 2025 and its framing as a second-term clemency action are incorrect.
description_long: Trump granted former Maricopa County sheriff Joe Arpaio a full and unconditional pardon on August 25, 2017. Arpaio had been convicted of criminal contempt for defying a federal court order in the Melendres racial-profiling case. The supplied correction identifies both a White House press release and a signed pardon warrant dated August 25 as records of the action. The event therefore concerns a first-term clemency decision, not a January 20, 2025 pardon at the start of Trump's second term. Its significance lies in the president's decision to pardon contempt arising from a sheriff's failure to obey a court order. That relationship links the use of clemency to judicial enforcement in a civil-rights case. The source material does not justify treating the pardon as a finding that Arpaio's conduct was lawful or that the underlying order lacked validity. The explanation records the conviction context, the president's action and its correct timing.

title: Foreign Governments Spend Millions at Trump-Owned Properties During Presidency
description_short: Foreign Governments Spend Millions at Trump-Owned Properties During Presidency
description_medium: Records later obtained by congressional investigators showed that foreign governments made millions of dollars in payments to Trump-owned businesses while Donald Trump was president. House Oversight Democrats reported at least $7.8 million from 20 governments through four properties. Lawsuits and congressional reports argued that such payments implicated the Foreign Emoluments Clause, but the litigation did not produce a final merits judgment establishing a constitutional violation. The legal conclusion should therefore be attributed rather than stated as adjudicated fact.
description_long: Congressional investigators obtained records of foreign-government payments to Trump-owned businesses during his first presidency. House Oversight Democrats reported at least $7.8 million from 20 governments through four properties. The figures should remain attributed to the committee's Democratic investigators and described as the documented amount they identified, rather than a comprehensive total for every Trump business. The payment relationship raised constitutional questions because Trump continued to own businesses receiving revenue while serving as president. Lawsuits and congressional reports argued that such payments implicated the Foreign Emoluments Clause. Those arguments are part of the accountability record, but they are not equivalent to a final court ruling. The supplied correction says the litigation produced no final merits judgment establishing a constitutional violation. This entry therefore distinguishes the financial evidence from the legal interpretation attached to it. It supports reporting the payments and the resulting allegations while avoiding the unsupported claim that the constitutional issue was finally adjudicated.

title: Foreign governments and foreign-government-linked entities spent money at Trump properties during his presidency, prompting Emoluments Clause litigation
description_short: Foreign governments and foreign-government-linked entities spent money at Trump properties during his presidency, prompting Emoluments Clause litigation
description_medium: Records and congressional investigations documented substantial foreign-government and foreign-government-linked spending at Trump properties during his first presidency. Saudi-linked lobbying activity included roughly $270,000 in Trump hotel charges spanning late 2016 into March 2017, and later congressional records documented additional foreign-government spending. Multiple lawsuits alleged that Trump's continued receipt of such business revenue violated the Constitution's Emoluments Clauses, but the Supreme Court ultimately directed dismissal of major cases as moot after he left office rather than resolving the constitutional merits.
description_long: Records and congressional investigations documented foreign-government and foreign-government-linked spending at Trump properties during his first presidency. One identified episode involved roughly $270,000 in Trump hotel charges from Saudi-linked lobbying activity spanning late 2016 into March 2017. The time window straddled the transition into office, so it should not all be described as spending during the presidency without qualification. Later congressional records documented additional foreign-government payments. These arrangements prompted lawsuits alleging that Trump's continuing receipt of business revenue violated the Constitution's Emoluments Clauses. The existence of those allegations and the evidence of spending are supported, but their constitutional merits were not finally resolved in the major cases described here. After Trump left office, the Supreme Court directed dismissal of those cases as moot. That procedural outcome did not establish either that the payments were constitutional or that they violated the clauses. The explanation therefore keeps the documented spending, the allegations and the litigation's disposition separate.
